hints: Think how to convert a gas volume measured under room conditions into moles, recall the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at room conditions.
Think how to convert moles of $\mathrm{H_2}$ into actual number of molecules using the Avogadro constant.
walkthrough:
Turn gas volume into moles**
You have $462 \, \mathrm{cm^3}$ of hydrogen collected at room conditions. For any gas at room conditions one mole occupies $24000 \, \mathrm{cm^3}$. So divide volume by molar volume:
$$n(\mathrm{H_2}) = \frac{462}{24000} = 0.01925 \, \mathrm{mol}$$

Turn moles into molecules**
One mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles. Multiply moles by the Avogadro constant:
$$N = 0.01925 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.16 \times 10^{22} \, \text{molecules}$$

hints: Write the cathode half-equation for formation of $\mathrm{H_2}$ from $\mathrm{H^+}$ and see how many electrons are needed per $\mathrm{H_2}$ molecule.
walkthrough:
Use the electron ratio per molecule**
Picture what happens at the cathode: $2\mathrm{H^+} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2}$. Each single $\mathrm{H_2}$ molecule needs 2 electrons to form. So simply double your answer from (a):
$$N(\mathrm{e^-}) = 2 \times 1.16 \times 10^{23} = 2.32 \times 10^{22}$$

hints: Recall the charge carried by a single electron and how total charge is built up from number of electrons.
walkthrough:
Multiply particles by charge per particle**
Each electron carries $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \, \mathrm{C}$. Total charge is number of electrons times charge per electron:
$$Q = N \times e = 2.32 \times 10^{22} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.71 \times 10^{3} \, \mathrm{C}$$

hints: Link charge, current and time with $Q = It$ and remember to convert the electrolysis time into seconds.
walkthrough:
Rearrange to find current**
Current is charge per second, $I = Q/t$. Time must be in seconds: $14.0 \, \mathrm{min} = 14.0 \times 60 = 840 \, \mathrm{s}$.
$$I = \frac{3.71 \times 10^{3}}{840} = 4.42 \, \mathrm{A}$$
That is your $x$, about $4.4 \, \mathrm{A}$.

hints: Apply $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum S^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$ and remember to multiply each $S^{\ominus}$ by its balancing number.
walkthrough:
Weight entropies by moles then subtract**
For $2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$:
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [2S^{\ominus}(\mathrm{H_2}) + S^{\ominus}(\mathrm{O_2})] - [2S^{\ominus}(\mathrm{H_2O})]$$
$$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [2(131) + 205] - [2(70)] = 467 - 140 = +327 \, \mathrm{J \, K^{-1} \, mol^{-1}}$$
The positive sign makes sense because you make 3 moles of disordered gas from ordered liquid.

hints: Recall the Gibbs equation linking $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$, temperature and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$.

Check units before substituting, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ is in $\mathrm{kJ \, mol^{-1}}$ while $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is in $\mathrm{J \, K^{-1} \, mol^{-1}}$, so convert $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ to $\mathrm{kJ}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Gibbs equation**
Free energy tells you feasibility:
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$

Substitute with matched units**
$\Delta H^{\ominus} = +572 \, \mathrm{kJ \, mol^{-1}}$, $T = 298 \, \mathrm{K}$, $\Delta S^{\ominus} = 327 \, \mathrm{J \, K^{-1} \, mol^{-1}} = 0.327 \, \mathrm{kJ \, K^{-1} \, mol^{-1}}$.
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 572 - (298 \times 0.327) = 572 - 97.4 = +474.6 \, \mathrm{kJ \, mol^{-1}}$$
Large positive $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ means non-spontaneous at 298 K, which is why electrical work is needed.
Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus} = 572 - (298 \times 0.327) = +475 \, \mathrm{kJ \, mol^{-1}}$ (accept $+474.6$)

hints: Look at the sign of $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ from (e)(i) and think how the $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ term in $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ changes as T rises.
walkthrough:
See which term wins at high T**
Here both $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ are positive. In $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$, raising T makes $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ larger and $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ more negative. So $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ falls and the splitting of water becomes more feasible, more spontaneous, at high temperature.

Final answer: Reaction becomes more spontaneous / feasible at higher T as $T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more positive so $-T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ becomes more negative and $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ decreases.
